topics.label: AI Literacy & Capability
topics.description: Critical capabilities needed to become AI fluent — frameworks, competencies, and workforce readiness.

articles.title: A competency framework for digital public health in Europe: an updated scoping review | npj Digital Public Health - Nature
articles.snippet: A competency framework for digital public health in Europe: an updated scoping review | npj Digital Public Health  Nature
articles.generalisability: Moderate — focused on European digital public health context; findings on competency frameworks may not fully transfer to other regions with different healthcare systems, regulatory environments, or digital infrastructure maturity.
takeaways: Identify which digital competencies (technical, data literacy, change management, privacy/security awareness) are most critical for your public health workforce, using the framework as a structured reference rather than assuming all competencies are equally important.

Design targeted upskilling programmes that address gaps in your organisation's current capability baseline, prioritising competencies that enable staff to work effectively with digital tools relevant to your specific public health challenges.

Use the framework to clarify role-specific competency expectations — different staff levels (frontline, supervisory, leadership) will need different depths of AI and digital literacy to function effectively.

articles.title: AI literacy in undergraduate medical education: a competency-based interpretive framework for curriculum and assessment - Frontiers
articles.snippet: AI literacy in undergraduate medical education: a competency-based interpretive framework for curriculum and assessment  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Moderate — focuses on medical education curriculum framework, which may not directly translate to general workforce AI literacy development, though competency-based approach principles could apply across sectors.
takeaways: Competency-based frameworks for AI literacy should include both technical understanding and clinical application — use this structure to design role-specific AI learning pathways for your organisation rather than generic AI training.

Medical education's emphasis on assessment alongside curriculum suggests pairing AI literacy training with practical competency checks (e.g., case-based tasks, decision-making scenarios) to embed learning rather than relying on knowledge tests alone.

The interpretive framework approach acknowledges contextual differences in how AI competencies apply across roles — adapt this method to map AI literacy needs for different job functions in your workplace.

articles.title: Integration of artificial intelligence competencies into a holistic digital literacy framework for middle school education - Nature
articles.snippet: Integration of artificial intelligence competencies into a holistic digital literacy framework for middle school education  Nature
articles.generalisability: Moderate — focuses on middle school education context; applicability to adult workplace AI literacy development requires interpretation and adaptation.
takeaways: A holistic digital literacy framework should integrate AI competencies alongside existing digital skills (data literacy, computational thinking, cybersecurity) rather than treating AI as a standalone module.

For adult learners, consider scaffolding AI literacy through foundational digital competencies first, ensuring employees have prerequisite skills before advancing to AI-specific knowledge and applications.

articles.title: From resistance to readiness: faculty development as the key to AI literacy in public health - Frontiers
articles.snippet: From resistance to readiness: faculty development as the key to AI literacy in public health  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Limited — focuses on public health faculty development context; findings may not transfer directly to other sectors or non-academic settings. Geographic scope unclear from title alone.
takeaways: Faculty development programs can shift mindsets from AI resistance to readiness; design interventions that address fears and build confidence before expecting AI adoption in curricula.

Public health educators need structured support to develop AI literacy themselves before teaching it; invest in train-the-trainer approaches and ongoing professional development rather than one-off workshops.
Moving staff from resistance to readiness requires engagement with underlying concerns; use change management principles and peer learning to normalize AI capabilities in health education contexts.

articles.title: The application of artificial intelligence in the context of person-centred care – a discourse on pitfalls and possibilities - Frontiers
articles.snippet: The application of artificial intelligence in the context of person-centred care – a discourse on pitfalls and possibilities  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Moderate — discourse-based review likely drawing on global literature, but no information provided on geographic scope, sample selection, or sector specificity. Findings may vary significantly depending on healthcare system context.
takeaways: Identify and document specific pitfalls (bias, loss of human connection, over-reliance on automation) before implementing AI tools in your organisation's care delivery to design mitigating safeguards.

Map how AI can enhance rather than replace person-centred care by clarifying which tasks benefit from automation (data analysis, administrative work) versus which require human judgment (relationship-building, ethical decisions).
Use this framework to audit existing or planned AI implementations against person-centred care principles to ensure technology serves the individual rather than organisational convenience.

articles.title: AI literacy as a meta-skill: a four-domain model for academic management innovation in higher education - Frontiers
articles.snippet: AI literacy as a meta-skill: a four-domain model for academic management innovation in higher education  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Moderate — proposes a conceptual framework for higher education contexts, but generalisability to other sectors (corporate, public service) and geographic regions unclear from snippet alone.
takeaways: Use the four-domain model as a structured framework to design AI literacy programs that go beyond technical skills — identify which domains (likely cognitive, technical, ethical, and organisational/change management) are weakest in your workforce and target development accordingly.

Position AI literacy as a meta-skill that enables employees to learn and adapt to new AI tools continuously, rather than training people on specific tools — this is more future-proof as AI capabilities evolve rapidly.

topics.label: AI & Organisational Psychology
topics.description: Impact of AI on wellbeing, engagement, job crafting, trust, and other org psych constructs.

articles.title: The double-edged mechanism of organizational AI adoption on employee creativity - Frontiers
articles.snippet: The double-edged mechanism of organizational AI adoption on employee creativity  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Unclear from snippet — geographic scope and sample characteristics not provided. Generalisation depends on sector diversity, organisational size, and cultural context of study sample.
takeaways: AI adoption in organisations can both enhance and constrain employee creativity depending on implementation context — organisations should assess whether their AI deployment supports creative autonomy or creates rigid processes that stifle innovation.
When introducing AI tools, clarify role boundaries and preserve space for creative problem-solving; over-reliance on AI automation may reduce employees' intrinsic motivation and creative engagement.

articles.title: Work autonomy mediates associations between medical AI readiness and well being in a three wave nurse study - Nature
articles.snippet: Work autonomy mediates associations between medical AI readiness and well being in a three wave nurse study  Nature
articles.generalisability: Findings are specific to nursing roles in medical settings. Generalisability to other professions or healthcare contexts is uncertain without details on sample size, geographic scope, and sector diversity. Results may not transfer to non-clinical or non-healthcare AI implementations.
takeaways: Preserve and actively protect work autonomy when implementing medical AI systems — autonomy appears to be the key mechanism linking AI readiness to employee wellbeing, so top-down AI adoption without staff input may undermine both acceptance and mental health outcomes.

Frame AI readiness training around how systems augment rather than replace clinical judgment; nurses' sense of control and decision-making authority during AI integration directly influences their wellbeing, not just their technical competence.

Use multi-wave implementation timelines with autonomy-preserving checkpoints rather than rapid rollout; the longitudinal design suggests wellbeing effects unfold over time, so staged adoption with staff feedback loops can mitigate negative trajectories.

articles.title: The impact of AI service quality on researchers’ work wellbeing: a dual-path moderated mediation model - Frontiers
articles.snippet: The impact of AI service quality on researchers’ work wellbeing: a dual-path moderated mediation model  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Limited — appears to focus on researchers as a specific occupational group, but geographic scope and sample size are unclear from the snippet provided. Findings may not generalise to other knowledge workers or organisational contexts.
takeaways: AI service quality directly affects researcher wellbeing through multiple pathways; audit your organisation's AI tools for usability, reliability, and support to identify barriers to adoption and wellbeing.

The dual-path model suggests both direct effects (tool functionality) and indirect effects (e.g. through workload or autonomy) matter; address both technical quality and how AI implementation shapes job design to maximise wellbeing outcomes.

Consider moderation factors (e.g. user experience, training readiness, role fit) when rolling out AI — a one-size-fits-all approach to AI service quality may miss critical contextual differences affecting researcher engagement and wellbeing.

articles.title: When AI works, employees worry: the vigilance cost of AI delegation in hybrid work - Frontiers
articles.snippet: When AI works, employees worry: the vigilance cost of AI delegation in hybrid work  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Scope unclear from snippet alone. Findings on AI delegation vigilance costs in hybrid work may be limited by sample geography, organisational context, and type of AI systems studied. Hybrid work prevalence varies globally, potentially affecting applicability.
takeaways: When delegating tasks to AI in hybrid settings, employees experience cognitive vigilance costs (monitoring, checking, verifying outputs) that can offset productivity gains—build in explicit handoff protocols and confidence thresholds to reduce unnecessary oversight.

Remote and hybrid workers may experience higher anxiety about AI decision-making due to physical distance from outcomes; consider targeted trust-building interventions and transparency about AI system reliability for distributed teams.

Monitor employee wellbeing metrics (stress, cognitive load) when introducing AI delegation tools, as the vigilance burden may create hidden fatigue costs not captured in task completion metrics alone.

articles.title: Crafting work with AI: human–AI collaborative job crafting, human–AI fit, and employee job performance - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Crafting work with AI: human–AI collaborative job crafting, human–AI fit, and employee job performance  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on sample size and sector diversity, which are not evident from the title and snippet. The concept of human–AI collaborative job crafting is theoretically relevant across knowledge work sectors, but empirical findings may be limited by the specific organisational context and AI tools studied.
takeaways: Encourage employees to actively shape how they work with AI tools rather than passively adopting them — collaborative job crafting (modifying tasks, relationships, and meaning around AI use) can improve fit and performance.
Assess and improve human–AI fit by understanding how well employees' skills, preferences, and workflows align with the AI tools available; misalignment is a barrier to effective AI adoption.
Frame AI implementation as an opportunity for role redesign: support employees in identifying which tasks to delegate to AI, which to keep, and how to redirect time toward higher-value work.

articles.title: Organizational psychological ownership drives employee-AI collaboration via AI crafting under paternalistic leadership - Nature
articles.snippet: Organizational psychological ownership drives employee-AI collaboration via AI crafting under paternalistic leadership  Nature
articles.generalisability: Generalisability unclear without access to full article. Findings may be context-specific to paternalistic leadership cultures (more common in East Asian organisations) and may not transfer to organisations with different leadership styles or cultural contexts.
takeaways: Foster psychological ownership of AI tools by involving employees in 'AI crafting' (customising or adapting AI to their specific workflows) — this can increase willingness to collaborate with AI systems.

In paternalistic leadership contexts, emphasise the leader's vision for AI as a protective, supportive tool rather than a replacement threat — this framing may strengthen employee buy-in and AI adoption.

Consider how your organisation's leadership style shapes AI adoption; the mechanisms that drive collaboration may differ significantly between paternalistic, transactional, and participative leadership models.

topics.label: Behavioural Change Frameworks
topics.description: Evidence-based frameworks for driving behaviour change — in the context of AI adoption and workforce transformation.

articles.title: AI adoption to adaptation: How a new change approach can build the human behaviors needed for AI - Deloitte
articles.snippet: AI adoption to adaptation: How a new change approach can build the human behaviors needed for AI  Deloitte
articles.generalisability: Limited — Deloitte reports typically draw on client work and consulting experience but lack transparent methodological details or independent validation. Findings may reflect practices among large organisations that engage Deloitte rather than broader workforce populations.
takeaways: Shift from viewing AI adoption as a one-time technology rollout to a continuous adaptation process that deliberately builds new behaviours and mindsets in staff over time.

Design change initiatives that address the human side of AI integration—such as how people work with AI tools, what skills they need, and how teams collaborate—rather than focusing solely on technical implementation.
Use structured behaviour-change methods to help employees move beyond initial AI awareness to sustained, practical engagement with AI capabilities in their daily work.

articles.title: How AI Is Reshaping the Future of Work - Stanford Graduate School of Business
articles.snippet: How AI Is Reshaping the Future of Work  Stanford Graduate School of Business
articles.generalisability: Limited — appears to be a Stanford GSB perspective piece without empirical data or specified geographic scope. Insights may reflect US business school thinking but applicability to Australian workplace contexts is unclear.
takeaways: Identify which roles in your organisation are most vulnerable to AI displacement and prioritise upskilling interventions for those cohorts before changes accelerate.

Establish clear communication about AI's role in your workplace to reduce anxiety-driven resistance; employees who understand AI as a tool rather than a replacement show greater willingness to engage with new systems.

articles.title: From adoption to impact: Three horizons of AI transformation - McKinsey & Company
articles.snippet: From adoption to impact: Three horizons of AI transformation  McKinsey & Company
articles.generalisability: Moderate — based on McKinsey's consulting experience across sectors, but findings reflect their client base (typically large enterprises) and may not generalise to small-to-medium businesses or non-corporate settings.
takeaways: Map your organisation's AI transformation across three distinct phases (adoption, scaling, impact) to clarify which stage you're in and what behaviour changes are needed at each level — this helps prioritise interventions rather than treating AI adoption as a single event.

Align leadership, capability-building, and cultural shifts explicitly at each horizon; misalignment (e.g., pushing impact-level changes before adoption fundamentals are in place) is a common reason transformation stalls.

Use the three-horizon framework to communicate change narratives to different employee groups — frontline staff need to understand their immediate adoption role, middle managers need to see scaling opportunities, and executives need clarity on business impact timelines.

articles.title: Dual-path mechanism of AI awareness on employee job crafting: insights from the cognitive appraisal of stress and JD-R perspective - Nature
articles.snippet: Dual-path mechanism of AI awareness on employee job crafting: insights from the cognitive appraisal of stress and JD-R perspective  Nature
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on sample characteristics not evident from title/snippet. The JD-R (Job Demands-Resources) framework is well-established across sectors, but findings may be specific to the organisation(s) and employee populations studied. Geographic scope and sector representation unclear.
takeaways: AI awareness triggers job crafting through two distinct pathways: threat appraisal (stress response) and opportunity appraisal (engagement response). Managers should monitor which pathway dominates in their teams and tailor communication to reframe AI as opportunity rather than threat.

The cognitive appraisal of AI—not AI itself—drives behaviour change. Invest in helping employees reappraise AI risks as manageable challenges and benefits as opportunities relevant to their role, rather than simply informing them AI exists.

Job crafting (how employees reshape their roles) is a key mechanism for managing AI-related stress. Create space for employees to proactively modify their tasks and responsibilities in response to AI, rather than imposing top-down role changes.

articles.title: Innovative technologies and workplace collaborations in the energy sector based in the United Arab Emirates - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Innovative technologies and workplace collaborations in the energy sector based in the United Arab Emirates  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Limited — findings specific to UAE energy sector context; applicability to Australian workplace settings and other sectors requires careful consideration of cultural, regulatory, and industry differences.
takeaways: Examine how your organisation's energy or resource sector can adopt collaboration technologies to support behaviour change in cross-functional teams.
Consider UAE energy sector case studies as one model, but test recommendations against Australian workplace norms, safety regulations, and team dynamics before implementation.

articles.title: AI Transformation Is a Workforce Transformation - Boston Consulting Group
articles.snippet: AI Transformation Is a Workforce Transformation  Boston Consulting Group
articles.generalisability: Moderate — BCG analysis likely draws on global client work and case studies, but the specific geographic scope, sample size, and methodological approach are unclear from the title and snippet alone. Findings may reflect practices among large organisations that engage consulting firms.
takeaways: AI adoption requires simultaneous changes to workforce skills, roles, and organisational structures — treat technology implementation as a catalyst for behaviour and capability change, not merely a tool deployment.
Design workforce transformation initiatives (training, reskilling, team restructuring) in parallel with AI rollout to reduce resistance and ensure people can actually use new systems effectively.

Identify which roles will change, disappear, or be created by AI early; communicate this transparently and invest in reskilling pathways to maintain engagement and psychological safety during transition.

topics.label: Fascinating Psychology Research
topics.description: Surprising, counterintuitive, and delightful findings from personality and behaviour research — the kind of study you'd share at dinner.

articles.title: Brain scans reveal a shocking difference between psychopaths and other people - Science Daily
articles.snippet: Brain scans reveal a shocking difference between psychopaths and other people  Science Daily
articles.generalisability: Limited — headline sensationalism typical of science news reporting; actual study details and sample characteristics not provided in snippet, making it impossible to assess generalisability without accessing the full article.
takeaways: Brain imaging studies consistently show structural or functional differences in psychopaths' brains (often in regions linked to emotion processing), but these differences don't fully explain or predict psychopathic behaviour — a reminder that neuroscience rarely offers simple biological explanations for complex personality traits.

The term 'psychopath' is often misused in popular media; clinical psychopathy is rare and distinct from general antisocial behaviour, which makes sensationalised headlines about 'shocking' brain differences worth approaching with healthy scepticism.

Brain scans are fascinating but can feel misleadingly definitive — colourful neuroimaging is powerful and persuasive to audiences, even when the findings are preliminary, small-scale, or don't yet translate to real-world applications.

articles.title: How a twin study untangled the surprising roots of authoritarian political beliefs - PsyPost
articles.snippet: How a twin study untangled the surprising roots of authoritarian political beliefs  PsyPost
articles.generalisability: Limited by reliance on twin study methodology, which assumes equal environments for identical and fraternal twins — an assumption often violated in practice. Geographic scope and sample composition not specified from snippet alone.
takeaways: Twin studies can tease apart nature vs. nurture contributions to political beliefs, revealing that authoritarianism has a heritable component — counterintuitive because we often assume politics is purely learned.
The finding challenges the idea that authoritarian attitudes are simply absorbed from parents or culture; genetic predispositions appear to play a measurable role alongside environmental factors.
This research reminds us that deeply held political convictions aren't uniformly 'chosen' — some people may be temperamentally predisposed toward hierarchical or rule-following worldviews.

articles.title: New psychology research shows the surprising romantic advantage of antagonistic narcissism - PsyPost
articles.snippet: New psychology research shows the surprising romantic advantage of antagonistic narcissism  PsyPost
articles.generalisability: Limited — snippet provides insufficient detail on study design, sample size, geographic scope, or methodology to assess generalisability.
takeaways: Antagonistic narcissism (dominance, hostility, entitlement) appears to confer a short-term romantic advantage, likely because assertiveness and confidence are initially attractive — even when paired with less likeable traits.
The finding is counterintuitive because narcissism is typically associated with relationship dysfunction, suggesting that what works for initial attraction may backfire once relationships develop.
This highlights a fundamental mismatch in human mating psychology: traits that signal reproductive fitness or status in brief encounters can undermine long-term partnership success.

articles.title: Musical preferences unite personalities across the globe - University of Cambridge
articles.snippet: Musical preferences unite personalities across the globe  University of Cambridge
articles.generalisability: Likely high — global research on music preferences suggests broad applicability across cultures, though specific sample composition and methodology not detailed in snippet.
takeaways: People's taste in music correlates with personality traits in remarkably consistent ways across different countries and cultures, suggesting personality-music links are universal rather than culturally determined.

Your playlist might be a surprisingly accurate window into your personality — a counterintuitive finding that what you choose to listen to reveals stable psychological patterns shared by billions of other humans.

This work hints that music preferences tap into something fundamental about how human personalities organise themselves, making it fascinating evidence for the universality of personality itself across vastly different societies.

articles.title: How good is the Myers-Briggs Type Indicator for predicting leadership-related behaviors? - Frontiers
articles.snippet: How good is the Myers-Briggs Type Indicator for predicting leadership-related behaviors?  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Moderate — reviews existing research on MBTI validity, but findings depend on the quality and scope of studies reviewed; MBTI's predictive power for leadership varies across contexts.
takeaways: Despite its ubiquity in corporate training, MBTI has surprisingly weak empirical support for predicting actual leadership behaviours — a finding that challenges decades of workplace popularity.

The mismatch between MBTI's widespread use and its limited scientific validation raises an interesting question: why do organisations keep using personality typing systems that don't robustly predict what they claim to measure?

This research highlights a fun paradox in human nature — we're drawn to neat personality categories (like MBTI) even when evidence suggests they're not particularly good forecasting tools for real-world performance.

articles.title: An AI analyzed wine reviews and found a surprising link to personality - PsyPost
articles.snippet: An AI analyzed wine reviews and found a surprising link to personality  PsyPost
articles.generalisability: Unclear from snippet — sample size, geographic scope, and methodology not provided. Findings may be limited to English-language wine reviews from specific platforms or regions.
takeaways: AI can detect personality traits from how people describe their subjective experiences — the language someone uses to review wine reveals patterns about who they are, not just their taste in wine.
This finding is counterintuitive because wine reviews seem purely about sensory description, yet personality bleeding through into everyday writing is universal and measurable.
It's a fun reminder that we're constantly leaking information about ourselves through our word choices, even when we think we're just talking about something concrete like wine.

topics.label: Psychological Safety
topics.description: Research on psychological safety and its role in team learning, AI experimentation, and innovation.

articles.title: Global Workforce Hopes and Fears Survey 2026 - PwC
articles.snippet: Global Workforce Hopes and Fears Survey 2026  PwC
articles.generalisability: High — large global sample across multiple countries and sectors, though specific country breakdowns and sample composition not detailed in snippet. Findings reflect worker attitudes at a single point in time (2026) and may not capture longer-term trends.
takeaways: Identify which specific workforce fears (e.g., job security, AI displacement, workload) are most prevalent in your organisation by comparing your results against PwC's global benchmarks to prioritise psychological safety interventions.

Use the survey's documented hopes and fears as a framework for employee listening sessions or focus groups to validate which concerns are most acute in your context and co-design safety initiatives that address them.

Monitor shifts in worker sentiment year-on-year by tracking your organisation against PwC's global trends, enabling early detection of emerging psychological safety risks before they escalate into engagement or retention issues.

articles.title: The dark side of artificial intelligence adoption: linking artificial intelligence adoption to employee depression via psychological safety and ethical leadership | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications - Nature
articles.snippet: The dark side of artificial intelligence adoption: linking artificial intelligence adoption to employee depression via psychological safety and ethical leadership | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications  Nature
articles.generalisability: Scope unclear from title and snippet alone, but findings about psychological safety and ethical leadership mechanisms are likely applicable across organisations adopting AI, though generalisability depends on sample characteristics (sector, geography, organisation size) not evident from the snippet provided.
takeaways: When introducing AI systems, proactively foster psychological safety — employees who feel unsafe to voice concerns about AI implementation are at higher risk of depression and disengagement; establish forums where staff can openly discuss AI-related anxieties without fear of dismissal or performance consequences.

Model and enforce ethical AI leadership from senior management — leaders who transparently address the ethical implications of AI adoption and demonstrate commitment to fair, responsible implementation can buffer against the negative mental health impacts of technological change.

Monitor employee wellbeing during AI transitions as a key performance indicator, not an afterthought — depression linked to AI adoption may signal underlying failures in change management, psychological safety, or leadership credibility that require intervention.

articles.title: Psychological Safety Levels the Playing Field for Employees - Boston Consulting Group
articles.snippet: Psychological Safety Levels the Playing Field for Employees  Boston Consulting Group
articles.generalisability: Moderate — BCG draws on their consulting experience across global clients, but specific sample composition, methodology, and data sources are not detailed in the snippet. Findings likely reflect practices in large, multinational organizations.
takeaways: Create structured opportunities for quieter or marginalized employees to contribute (e.g., written input channels, small-group discussions, rotating speaking roles) to ensure psychological safety benefits all team members, not just extroverts.
Measure and track psychological safety as a leading indicator of team performance and inclusion; teams with higher psychological safety show more diverse participation and better problem-solving.
Leaders should explicitly model vulnerability and acknowledge mistakes to normalize risk-taking; this signals that the organization values honesty over performative perfection.

articles.title: 4 Ways Leaders Can Build 'Psychological Safety' in Their Work Teams - SHRM
articles.snippet: 4 Ways Leaders Can Build 'Psychological Safety' in Their Work Teams  SHRM
articles.generalisability: Moderate — SHRM content is US-focused, though psychological safety principles are broadly applicable. Leadership practices may need adaptation for different organisational cultures and Australian employment contexts.
takeaways: Identify which of the four specific leader behaviours (likely acknowledgement of mistakes, soliciting input, responding constructively to concerns, and role modelling vulnerability) your team most needs, then pilot one consistently over 4–6 weeks to establish trust before adding others.

Use psychological safety diagnostics (anonymous pulse surveys or focus groups) to establish a baseline before and after implementing leader changes, so you can measure whether your interventions are actually shifting team behaviour and willingness to speak up.

articles.title: The work affective well-being under the impact of AI - Nature
articles.snippet: The work affective well-being under the impact of AI  Nature
articles.generalisability: Cannot be fully assessed from the snippet provided — the title suggests a study on AI's emotional impact at work, but details on sample size, geography, sector, and methodology are not visible in the excerpt.
takeaways: Monitor and measure employee emotional responses to AI implementation — anxiety, stress, or disengagement during AI rollout may signal psychological safety concerns that need proactive addressing.

Consider affective well-being as a key outcome when designing AI adoption strategies; neglecting emotional impact risks undermining both psychological safety and the effectiveness of AI capability development initiatives.

articles.title: Empowering workforces in AI-driven environments: co-skilling, organizational support, and mitigating job insecurity - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Empowering workforces in AI-driven environments: co-skilling, organizational support, and mitigating job insecurity  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Moderate — appears to synthesize existing research on AI adoption and workforce psychology, but without explicit detail on geographic scope or sector representation, applicability may vary across different organisational contexts and labour markets.
takeaways: Co-skilling programs that pair AI training with existing role responsibilities can reduce job insecurity and increase psychological safety by helping employees see AI as a tool to enhance rather than replace their work.

Organisational support structures—including transparent communication about AI implementation, clear career pathways, and manager training—are critical to building trust and psychological safety during AI transition periods.
Addressing job insecurity explicitly through honest dialogue and upskilling opportunities may be more effective at maintaining engagement and psychological safety than relying on reassurance alone.
